Meanwhile, modern systems lean on a cache to cut latency; a warm cache answers common queries fast, sparing disks. Databases pay dearly for random reads, so keeping hot rows in memory boosts throughput and trims cost across busy production stacks.

However, every cache brings risk: stale data. Invalidation is hard, and bugs hide there for months; a write must update or evict the copy, or users will read old values. Teams pick policies like LRU or TTL, tune sizes, watch hit ratios, and accept that a cache is merely a small bet on data locality.

Along with such gains, ops staff must watch RAM limits, hunt hot rows, and drop stall risks fast. A total flush drags all traffic back onto disks, so warming up again is vital; sysadmins rely on scripts, dry runs, and small backup lists.

Finally, treat a cache as an optimization, not a source of truth, and measure before tuning: correctness first, then done.
